nodes.name: (epsilon, delta)-local min-max point
nodes.origin_citation: Daskalakis & Panageas 2018; Heusel et al. 2017; Adolphs et al. 2018
nodes.statement_short: A point where neither player can improve f by more than epsilon within a delta-ball.

nodes.name: Local min-max points reduce to local minima in the small-delta regime
nodes.statement: In the ``local" regime where $\delta < O(\sqrt{\varepsilon})$, if $f \in [-1,1]$ with $O(1)$-Lipschitz gradient,  any point which is an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-local minimum of the function $f$ with respect to the variable $(x,y)$, or an $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-local maximum of $f$ with respect to $(x,y)$, will also be a $(\Omega(\varepsilon), O(\delta))$-local min-max point of this function; thus, in this regime the problem of finding local min-max points is equivalent  to the problem of finding a local minimum or maximum point.
conclusions: any point which is an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-local minimum of the function $f$ with respect to the variable $(x,y)$, or an $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-local maximum of $f$ with respect to $(x,y)$, will also be a $(\Omega(\varepsilon), O(\delta))$-local min-max point of this function
nodes.statement_short: For delta below sqrt(epsilon), local minima/maxima of f are local min-max points, so the problems are equivalent.

nodes.name: Nonexistence of local min-max points for large delta
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, outside of the regime $\delta < O(\sqrt{\varepsilon})$, local min-max points may not exist even for functions $f$ where the value of $f \in [-1,1]$ and $f$ is $O(1)$-Lipschitz with $O(1)$-Lipschitz gradient and Hessian.\footnote{For instance, the function $f(x,y) := \sin(x+y)$ has no $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-local min-max points when $\frac{1}{100} > \delta > \sqrt{\varepsilon}$.}
nodes.statement_short: For delta above sqrt(epsilon), local min-max points may fail to exist even for bounded smooth f, e.g. sin(x+y).

nodes.name: Polynomial-time convergence to approximate local minima
nodes.statement: \cite{nesterov2006cubic} and other recent works \cite{agarwal2017finding, allen2018natasha, NonconvexOptimizationForML, carmon2018accelerated, fang2018near, arjevani2020second}, have shown that one can find an $(\varepsilon, \theta)$-approximate local minimum in time roughly $\mathrm{poly}\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon},\log d, \frac{1}{\theta}, b, L\right)$ gradient evaluations.
nodes.origin_citation: Nesterov & Polyak 2006; Agarwal et al. 2017; Allen-Zhu 2018; Jin et al.; Carmon et al. 2018; Fang et al. 2018; Arjevani et al. 2020
also_stated_at: If $\psi$ is Lipschitz smooth and bounded, we will reach such a point in polynomial time from any starting point \cite{nesterov2006cubic, ge2015escaping}.
conclusions: one can find an $(\varepsilon, \theta)$-approximate local minimum in time roughly $\mathrm{poly}\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon},\log d, \frac{1}{\theta}, b, L\right)$ gradient evaluations
nodes.statement_short: Second-order methods find an (epsilon, theta)-approximate local minimum in poly(1/epsilon, log d, 1/theta, b, L) gradient evaluations.

nodes.name: C^2-smooth function
nodes.statement: In the following,  we say that a function is $C^2$-smooth if its second derivatives are continuous on its domain.
differentia: its second derivatives are continuous on its domain

nodes.name: Largest and smallest eigenvalue
nodes.statement: $\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}(A)$ denotes the largest eigenvalue of any square matrix $A$, and $\lambda_{\mathrm{min}}(A)$ is its smallest eigenvalue.

nodes.name: Euclidean norm and operator norm
nodes.statement: $\| \cdot \|$ denotes the Euclidean $\ell_2$ norm, and $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}} = \sup_{v \neq 0} \frac{v^\top A v}{\|v\|^{2}} $ the operator norm of any square matrix $A$.

nodes.name: Bounded objective with Lipschitz Hessian
nodes.statement_short: f is b-bounded and has L-Lipschitz Hessian.

nodes.name: Bounded function with Lipschitz Hessian is Lipschitz with Lipschitz gradient
nodes.statement_short: A b-bounded f with L-Lipschitz Hessian is L1-Lipschitz (L1 <= 4 b^{2/3} L^{1/3}) with L2-Lipschitz gradient (L2 <= 2 b^{1/3} L^{2/3}).

nodes.name: L1-Lipschitz function and L2-Lipschitz gradient
nodes.statement: We say $f: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is $L_1$-Lipschitz if $|f(x,y) -  f(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})| \leq L_1 \sqrt{\| x- \tilde{x}\|^2 + \| y- \tilde{y}\|^2}$, and that $f$ has $L_2$-Lipschitz gradient if $\|\nabla f(x,y) - \nabla f(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})\| \leq L_2 \sqrt{\| x- \tilde{x}\|^2 + \| y- \tilde{y}\|^2}$.

nodes.name: Exact local minimum
nodes.statement:
We say that a point $x^\star \in \mathbb{R}^d$  is an {\em exact} local minimum point of  a function  $\psi: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ if there exists $\delta>0$ such that 
 
\noindent
\begin{equation} \psi(x^\star) \leq \psi(x), \ \  \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d\textrm{ such that }\|x - x^\star \| \leq \delta.
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Exact local minimum condition
nodes.statement: \psi(x^\star) \leq \psi(x), \ \  \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d\textrm{ such that }\|x - x^\star \| \leq \delta.
nodes.label: eq:ExactLocalMin_formal

nodes.name: (epsilon, theta)-approximate local minimum
nodes.statement:
For any $\varepsilon, \theta \geq 0$, say that a point $x^\star$  is an $(\varepsilon, \theta)$-approximate local minimum for  a $C^2$-smooth function $\psi: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ if
    
    \noindent
\begin{equation} \|\nabla \psi(x^\star)\| \leq \varepsilon \qquad \mbox{and} \quad \lambda_{\mathrm{min}}( \nabla^2 \psi(x^\star)) \geq -\theta.
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Second-order approximate local minimum: gradient norm at most epsilon and smallest Hessian eigenvalue at least -theta.

nodes.name: Second-order approximate local minimum conditions
nodes.statement: \|\nabla \psi(x^\star)\| \leq \varepsilon \qquad \mbox{and} \quad \lambda_{\mathrm{min}}( \nabla^2 \psi(x^\star)) \geq -\theta.
nodes.label: eq:ApproximateLocalMin_formal

nodes.name: (epsilon, theta)-approximate local maximum
nodes.statement: We say that $x^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon, \theta)$-approximate local {\em maximum} of $\psi$ if  $x^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon, \theta)$-approximate local {\em minimum} of $-\psi$.

nodes.name: Greedy path
nodes.statement:
Let $x\in \mathbb{R}^d$, and suppose a continuous path $\varphi_t:[0,\tau] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ is differentiable except at a finite number of points, and at the points where it is differentiable $\left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \varphi_t \right\| = 1$ (i.e., the path travels at unit speed).  Then for any $\varepsilon \geq 0$, we say $\varphi$ is an $\varepsilon$-greedy path for $f(x, \cdot)$ if at all points where $\varphi$ is differentiable $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} f(x, \varphi_t)\geq - \varepsilon$ and

\begin{equation} \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} f(x, \varphi_t) >\varepsilon \qquad \textrm{ or } \qquad

 \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}t^2} f(x, \varphi_t) > \sqrt{L_{} \varepsilon}.

\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A unit-speed path along which f(x, .) never decreases faster than epsilon and either increases at rate > epsilon or has second derivative > sqrt(L epsilon).
nodes.label: def_greedy_path

nodes.name: Greedy path condition
nodes.statement:
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} f(x, \varphi_t) >\varepsilon \qquad \textrm{ or } \qquad

 \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}t^2} f(x, \varphi_t) > \sqrt{L_{} \varepsilon}.
nodes.label: eq_greedy_path

nodes.name: Set of greedy-path endpoints
nodes.statement:
Towards this end, we define the set $S_{\varepsilon, x, y} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ of endpoints of $\varepsilon$-greedy paths, for any $x,y \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $\varepsilon>0$. 
  
   We say that a point $z \in S_{\varepsilon, x, y}$ if there is a number $\tau \geq 0$ and a path $\varphi:[0,\tau] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ which is an $\varepsilon$-greedy path for $f(x,\cdot)$, with initial point $\varphi_0 = y$ and endpoint $\varphi_\tau = z$.
nodes.statement_short: S_{eps,x,y} is the set of endpoints of epsilon-greedy paths for f(x, .) started at y.

nodes.name: Greedy max function
nodes.statement_short: g_eps(x,y) is the supremum of f(x,z) over endpoints z of epsilon-greedy paths from y.

nodes.name: Greedy max function formula
nodes.statement: g_\varepsilon(x,y):= \sup \{f(x,z) : z\in  S_{\varepsilon, x, y}\}.
nodes.label: eq_greedy_max

nodes.name: Greedy paths can escape saddle points and local minima
nodes.statement:
Equations \eqref{eq_greedy_path} together ensure that for any  $y$ where either 

 (i) the gradient  $\nabla_y f(x,y)$ has magnitude greater than $\varepsilon$ or 

 (ii) the eigenvalues of the Hessian $\nabla_y^2 f(x,y)$ are bounded below by $-\sqrt{L_{} \varepsilon}$, there is always a unit-speed greedy path (with parameter $\varepsilon$) starting at $y$ which can increase the value of $f$ at an average rate
 
 \footnote{By ``average rate" of at least $\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon$ we mean that the increase in $f$ divided by the length of the path is $\geq \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon$.} 
 of at least $\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon$ by traveling a distance of at most $\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}{\sqrt{L_{}}}$. 

 Moreover, since one such greedy path is always a straight line in the direction of either the gradient $\nabla_y f(x,y)$ or 
  the largest eigenvector of $\nabla_y^2 f(x,y)$, all one needs to compute such a path is access to the gradient and Hessian of $f(x,\cdot)$. 
 
 This fact can also be viewed as a motivation for the definition of approximate local maximum (Inequality \eqref{eq:ApproximateLocalMin_formal}): roughly, any point
   which does not satisfy both conditions (i) and (ii) (up to a constant factor) is an approximate local maximum. 
  
   Thus, starting from any point $y$ which is not an approximate local maximum of $f(x, \cdot)$ (with parameters $(\varepsilon, \sqrt{L_{} \varepsilon})$), 
    there is always an easy-to-compute greedy path (with parameter $\varepsilon$) which allows one to increase the value of $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Away from approximate local maxima, a straight-line greedy path (gradient or top eigenvector) increases f at average rate epsilon/2.
nodes.label: rem_escaping_saddle_points

nodes.name: Approximate local minimum for discontinuous functions
nodes.statement:
For any $\varepsilon, \sigma \geq 0$, we say that $x^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum for a uniformly bounded function $\psi$ if
  \begin{equation} \| \nabla_{x}  \mathcal{S}(x^\star) \| \leq \varepsilon \qquad \textrm{ and } \qquad

 

   \lambda_{\mathrm{min}}( \nabla^2_{x}   \mathcal{S}(x^\star) ) \geq -\sqrt{\varepsilon},
  \end{equation}
  where $\mathcal{S}(x) := \mathbb{E}_{\zeta \sim N(0,I_d)}\left [\min(\psi(x  + \sigma \zeta),  \psi(x^\star)) \right].$
nodes.section: 2.2 Dealing with discontinuities and other difficulties of the greedy max function
nodes.statement_short: x* is an (epsilon, sigma)-approximate local minimum of a bounded psi if the Gaussian smoothing of min(psi, psi(x*)) has small gradient and Hessian bounded below at x*.

nodes.name: Greedy adversarial equilibrium
nodes.statement:
For any $\varepsilon, \sigma \geq 0$, we say that $(x^\star, y^\star)\in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-greedy adversarial equilibrium of a $C^2$-smooth function $f: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with $L$-Lipschitz Hessian, if we have

\begin{equation} \|\nabla_y f(x^\star, y^\star)\| \leq \varepsilon
 \quad \textrm{and} \quad

 \lambda_{\mathrm{max}}( \nabla^2_{y} f(x^\star, y^\star)) \leq \sqrt{L \varepsilon}, \textrm{ and }
\end{equation}


  \begin{equation} \| \nabla_{x} S(x^\star)\| \leq \varepsilon  \quad \textrm{ and }  \quad

 

 \lambda_{\mathrm{min}}( \nabla^2_{x} S(x^\star)) \geq -\sqrt{ \varepsilon},
   
  \end{equation} where $S(x) :=  \mathbb{E}_{\zeta \sim N(0,I_d)}\left [\min(g_\varepsilon(x  + \sigma \zeta, y^\star),  g_\varepsilon(x^\star, y^\star)) \right]$.
also_stated_at: We say that $(x^\star, y^\star)$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-greedy adversarial equilibrium of a function $f: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with $L$-Lipschitz Hessian if $y^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sqrt{L\varepsilon})$-approximate local maximum of $f(x^\star, \cdot)$ (in the sense of Inequality \eqref{eq:ApproximateLocalMin_formal}), and if $x^\star$  is an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum of the (possibly) discontinuous function $g_\varepsilon(\cdot, y^\star)$ (in the sense of Definition \ref{def_discontinuos_local_min}).
nodes.statement_short: y* is an approximate local max of f(x*, .) and x* an approximate local min of the truncated Gaussian-smoothed greedy max g_eps(., y*).

nodes.name: Main result: existence and efficient computation of greedy adversarial equilibria
nodes.statement:
Let $\varepsilon, \sigma>0$, with $\sigma \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon d}}$, and consider any $C^2$-smooth  uniformly bounded function $f: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with Lipschitz Hessian. 

 Then there exists a point $(x^\star, y^\star) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d$  which is an ($\varepsilon^\star, \sigma)$-greedy adversarial equilibrium for $f$, for some  $\varepsilon^\star \leq \varepsilon$.

Moreover, there exists an algorithm which, given access to oracles for the value of a $C^2$-smooth function $f: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow [-b,b]$, and to oracles for $\nabla_y f$ and $\nabla^2_y f$, where $f$ has $L_{}$-Lipschitz Hessian for some $b, L_{} >0$, and numbers $\varepsilon, \sigma \geq 0$, with probability at least $\frac{9}{10}$ generates a  point $(x^\star,y^\star) \in \mathbb{R}^{d} \times \mathbb{R}^{d}$ which is an $(\varepsilon^\star, \sigma)$-greedy adversarial equilibrium for $f$, for some  $\varepsilon^\star \leq \varepsilon$. 

 Moreover, this algorithm takes a number of gradient, Hessian, and function evaluations which is polynomial in $\frac{1}{\varepsilon}, d, b, L_{}, \frac{1}{\sigma}$.
assumptions: any $C^2$-smooth  uniformly bounded function $f: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with Lipschitz Hessian
conclusions: there exists a point $(x^\star, y^\star) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d$  which is an ($\varepsilon^\star, \sigma)$-greedy adversarial equilibrium for $f$, for some  $\varepsilon^\star \leq \varepsilon$

with probability at least $\frac{9}{10}$ generates a  point $(x^\star,y^\star) \in \mathbb{R}^{d} \times \mathbb{R}^{d}$ which is an $(\varepsilon^\star, \sigma)$-greedy adversarial equilibrium for $f$, for some  $\varepsilon^\star \leq \varepsilon$
this algorithm takes a number of gradient, Hessian, and function evaluations which is polynomial in $\frac{1}{\varepsilon}, d, b, L_{}, \frac{1}{\sigma}$
nodes.statement_short: Every bounded C^2 function with Lipschitz Hessian has an (epsilon, sigma)-greedy adversarial equilibrium, found w.p. 9/10 with poly(1/eps, d, b, L, 1/sigma) oracle calls.
nodes.label: thm:GreedyMin-max

nodes.name: Our second-order maximization algorithm computes an epsilon-greedy path
nodes.statement:
We have shown that at each point $p$ on a line segment $[z, z']$ connecting two consecutive steps $z$ and $z'$ of our maximization algorithm, we have that either  $\nabla_y f(x,p)^\top u > \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon$  or $u^\top \nabla_y^2 f(x,p) u > \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\varepsilon}$, where $u$ is the unit vector $u = \frac{z'-z}{\|z'-z\|}$.



 Therefore, at any point on the unit-speed path $\varphi_t$ made up of the line segments connecting the consecutive steps of our algorithm, we have that either $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} f(x, \varphi_t) > \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon$, or $\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}t^2} f(x, \varphi_t)  > \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\varepsilon}$.

This implies that the path traced by our algorithm is a $\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon$-greedy path. 


We show that, for a smaller choice of step sizes than required by \eqref{eq_mu1} and \eqref{eq_mu3}, namely for  $\mu_1, \mu_3 = \mathrm{poly}\left(\frac{1}{d}, \varepsilon\right) $, this path is $\varepsilon'$-greedy where $|\varepsilon- \varepsilon'| = \mathrm{poly}\left(\frac{1}{d}, \varepsilon\right)$.

 The fact that $\varepsilon' \neq \varepsilon$ causes some technical issues which we deal with in the full algorithm\footnote{In the full algorithm we deal with this issue by initially computing an $\varepsilon'$-greedy path for $\varepsilon' = \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ at the first iteration, and then slowly increasing $\varepsilon'$ at each iteration.} in Section \ref{sec:algorithm} and in our proof (Section 
 
 \ref{sec_proof_of_main_theorem}).  To improve readability, we ignore these issues in this technical overview and assume that the path is $\varepsilon$-greedy.

nodes.statement_short: The iterates of the maximization subroutine trace a (1/2)epsilon-greedy path; smaller step sizes make it epsilon'-greedy.

nodes.name: Max-player update leaves h_epsilon unchanged
nodes.statement:
Since $h_\varepsilon$ is the value of $f$ at the $(\varepsilon, \sqrt{ \varepsilon})$-approximate local maximum $y'$, we therefore have that $h_\varepsilon(w, y) = f(w, y')$.

Moreover, since $y'$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sqrt{ \varepsilon})$-approximate local maximum for $f$, and Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop} stops whenever it reaches an $(\varepsilon, \sqrt{ \varepsilon})$-approximate local maximum, $y'$ is a stationary point for Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop}, which means that $f(w, y') = h_\varepsilon(w, y')$.

Thus, 

\begin{equation} h_\varepsilon(w, y) = f(w, y') = h_\varepsilon(w, y').

\end{equation}

nodes.name: Convergence of the alternating scheme
nodes.statement: Thus, since the max-player's update does not change the value of $h_\varepsilon$  \eqref{h_unchanged}, if we can show that whenever $x$ is not an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum of $f(\cdot, y)$ the min player can find an update to $x$ which decreases the value of $h_\varepsilon(x,y)$ by at least some fixed amount $\gamma_1>0$, then we would have that the value of $h_\varepsilon$ decreases monotonically at each iteration by at least $\gamma_1$. In that case, our algorithm would have to converge after  $\frac{2b}{\gamma_1}$ iterations to a point $(x,y')$ where $x$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum for $h_\varepsilon(\cdot, y')$ and $y'$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sqrt{\varepsilon})$-approximate local maximum for $f(x,\cdot)$.

nodes.name: Gradient-free stochastic gradient Gamma
nodes.statement:
We use a stochastic gradient $\Gamma(w)$ for $s(w)$ which can be computed with access only to the value of $h_\varepsilon$; roughly

\begin{equation} \Gamma(w) = \frac{\zeta}{\sigma} \min\left(h_\varepsilon(w + \sigma \zeta, y), h_\varepsilon(x ,y)\right)
\end{equation}

where $\zeta \sim N(0, I_d)$, and $\mathbb{E}[ \Gamma(w)] = s(w)$ (see e.g. \cite{flaxman2005online}).

nodes.statement_short: Gamma(w) = (zeta/sigma) min(h_eps(w + sigma zeta, y), h_eps(x, y)), computable from values of h_eps only.

\begin{equation} w \leftarrow w -\eta \Gamma(w) + \alpha \xi
\end{equation}

where $\xi \sim N(0,I_d)$ and $\eta, \alpha$ are hyperparameters .

 \ref{prop_SGVariance}) to results about noisy SGD \cite{NonconvexOptimizationForML} to show that, whenever $x$ is not an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum for $h_\varepsilon(\cdot,y)$, with high probability, this noisy SGD, with hyperparameters $\eta, \alpha = \mathrm{poly}\left(\frac{1}{d}, \varepsilon\right)$, can find an update for $x$ which decreases the value of $h_\varepsilon$ by at least $\gamma_1=\mathrm{poly}\left(\frac{1}{d},  \varepsilon\right)$ after $\mathcal{I} =  \mathrm{poly}\left(d, \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)$ iterations of Equation \eqref{eq_noisySGD}    (Proposition \ref{Prop_NoisySGD}).

nodes.name: Proof of Idea 3
nodes.statement:
This is because, if $x^\star$ is an exact local minimum, then there is an open ball $B$ containing $x^\star$ where $h_\varepsilon(x^\star, y^\star) = \min_{w \in B} h_\varepsilon(w, y^\star)$.

This implies that
\begin{equation}
g_\varepsilon(x^\star, y^\star) \stackrel{\textrm{Eq.}\eqref{eq_Tech2}}{=} h_\varepsilon(x^\star, y^\star) = \min_{w \in B} h_\varepsilon(w, y^\star)

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the main result (runtime)
nodes.statement:
From Idea 1 we have that our algorithm terminates after $O\left(\frac{1}{\gamma_1}\right)$ iterations consisting of an update for the min-player and max-player, if one can bound by some number $\gamma_1>0$ the amount by which each update for the min-player decreases the value of $h_\varepsilon(x,y)$.

  From Idea 2 (Section \ref{sec_escape_saddle}) we have that, with high probability, noisy SGD can allow the min-player to find an update which decreases the value of $h_\varepsilon$ by an amount  $\gamma_1=\mathrm{poly}\left(\frac{1}{d},  \varepsilon\right)$, and that this can be accomplished in $\mathcal{I} =  \mathrm{poly}\left(d, \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)$  computations of $h_\varepsilon$.
 
 In Section \ref{sec_local_approx}, we show that our maximization subroutine can compute the value of $h_\varepsilon$ in at most $O\left(\frac{1}{\Delta}\right)$ oracle calls, where $\Delta = \min\left\{\frac{1}{2} \mu_1 \varepsilon^2, \frac{1}{2} (\mu_3)^2 \sqrt{\varepsilon}\right\}$.

From Equations \eqref{eq_mu1} and \eqref{eq_mu3}, roughly speaking, we may set $\mu_1 = \frac{1}{4}$ and $\mu_3 =  \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\varepsilon}$. \footnote{As mentioned in Remark \ref{rem_greedy_path}, in the full algorithm we use somewhat smaller hyperparameter values $\mu_1, \mu_3 = \mathrm{poly}(\frac{1}{d}, \varepsilon)$ to ensure that the path computed by Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop} is $\varepsilon$-greedy instead of $\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon$-greedy.}  

This means that, with high probability, the number of oracle calls until our algorithm terminates is 
$
O\left(\frac{1}{\Delta} \times \mathcal{I} \times \frac{1}{\gamma_1}\right) = \mathrm{poly}\left(d, \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right).
$

Finally, from Idea 1 we also have that, if our algorithm terminates, it returns a pair of points $(x^\star, y^\star)$ where $x^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum for $h_\varepsilon(\cdot, y^\star)$ (in the sense of Definition \ref{def_discontinuos_local_min}) and $y^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sqrt{ \varepsilon})$-approximate local maximum for $f(x^\star,\cdot)$ (in the sense of Equation \eqref{eq:ApproximateLocalMin_formal}).

Applying Idea 3 (or rather its extension to {\em approximate} local minima), we have that  $x^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum for $h_\varepsilon(\cdot, y^\star)$, which implies that $(x^\star, y^\star)$ is a $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-greedy adversarial equilibrium.

In other words, our algorithm returns an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-greedy adversarial equilibrium after at most $ \mathrm{poly}\left(d, \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)$ oracle calls for the gradient, Hessian, and value of $f$.

nodes.name: Summary of the greedy adversarial equilibrium algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Find an approximate local max y1, then repeatedly search by noisy SGD for x decreasing h_eps by gamma1 and re-maximize y; stop when no decrease is found.

nodes.name: Initial maximization
nodes.statement: Starting at the initial point $(x_0, y_0)$, our algorithm first uses the second-order optimization method described in Section \ref{sec_local_approx} (Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop}) to find a point $y_1$ which is an  $(\varepsilon, \sqrt{\varepsilon})$-approximate local maximum for $f(x_0, \cdot)$.
nodes.statement_short: Run Algorithm 1 from y0 to get y1.

nodes.name: Noisy SGD search for a decrease
nodes.statement_short: Search by noisy SGD with stochastic gradient Gamma for x_{i+1} decreasing h_eps by gamma1.

nodes.name: Stochastic gradient used in the summary algorithm
nodes.statement: \Gamma(w) = \frac{\zeta}{\sigma} \min \left(h_\varepsilon(w + \sigma \zeta, y_{i}), h_\varepsilon(x_i,y_{i})\right),

nodes.name: Update or stop
nodes.statement:
If our algorithm is able to find an update $x_{i+1}$ which satisfies Inequality \eqref{eq_decrease}, it uses Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop} to compute a point $y_{i+1}$, which is an $(\varepsilon, \sqrt{\varepsilon})$-approximate local maximum for $f(x_{i+1},\cdot)$,

 sets $i\leftarrow i+1$,  and goes back to Step 2.

  Otherwise, if it cannot find such an update, it concludes that $x_i$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum for $h_\varepsilon(\cdot ,y_{i}$), and, hence, that $(x_i,y_{i})$ is a  $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-greedy adversarial equilibrium.
nodes.statement_short: If a decrease is found re-maximize y and repeat; otherwise return (x_i, y_i).

Then for any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\sigma^\star>0$ such that for any $0< \sigma \leq \sigma^\star$,  $x^\star$ is an approximate local minimum for the function $\psi$ with smoothing $\sigma$.

nodes.name: Local min-max points are greedy adversarial equilibria
nodes.statement: Suppose that for any $\delta>0$, $(x^\star, y^\star)$ is a $(0, \delta)$-local min-max point for a $C^2$-smooth function $f: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, and that there is a number $b>0$ such that $|f(x,y)| \leq b$ for all $x,y \in \mathbb{R}^d$.  Then for any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists  $\sigma^\star>0$ such that for every $0< \sigma \leq  \sigma^\star$ we have that $(x^\star, y^\star)$ is a  $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-greedy adversarial equilibrium for $f$.

also_stated_at: Any point which is a local min-max point is also a greedy adversarial equilibrium for small enough $\sigma>0$ (Corollary \ref{corollary_exact_greedy_minmax}).

there is a number $b>0$ such that $|f(x,y)| \leq b$ for all $x,y \in \mathbb{R}^d$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.2
nodes.statement:
Any point $(x^\star, y^\star)$ which is a $(0, \delta)$-local min-max point has the property that $x^\star$ is an exact local minimum of $f(\cdot, y^\star)$ and that $y^\star$ is an exact local maximum of $f(x^\star, \cdot)$. 
  
    This implies that $y^\star$ is an approximate local maximum of $f(x^\star, \cdot)$ for parameter $\varepsilon$ and any parameter $\theta$ (in the sense of Inequality \eqref{eq:ApproximateLocalMin_formal}).  Thus, the only greedy path starting at $y^\star$ consists only of the point $\{y^\star\}$ itself, and hence we have that $g_\varepsilon(x^\star, y^\star) = f(x^\star, y^\star)$. 
  
    Therefore, since $g_\varepsilon(x,y) \geq f(x,y)$ for all $x,y$, the fact that $x^\star$ is  an exact local minimum of  $f(\cdot, y^\star)$ implies that it is also an exact local minimum of $g_\varepsilon(x^\star, y^\star)$. 
  
    By Lemma \ref{lemma_local_nash} we therefore have that there exists $\sigma^\star > 0$ such that $x^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum of $g_\varepsilon(\cdot, y^\star)$ for any $0<\sigma \leq \sigma^\star$  (in the sense of Definition \ref{def_discontinuos_local_min}). 
    
    
    Since $y^\star$ is an approximate local maximum of $f(x^\star, \cdot)$ for parameter $\varepsilon$ and any parameter $\theta$  (in the sense of Inequality \eqref{eq:ApproximateLocalMin_formal}) and  $x^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum of $g_\varepsilon(\cdot, y^\star)$ (in the sense of Definition \ref{def_discontinuos_local_min}), we must have that $(x^\star, y^\star)$ is an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-greedy adversarial equilibrium.

nodes.name: Convergence under sufficient bilinearity
nodes.statement:
For instance, \cite{abernethy2019last} show that if $f$ has $1$-Lipschitz gradient and satisfies a ``sufficient bilinearity'' condition-- that is, roughly speaking, if the cross derivative $
abla^2_{xy} f(x,y)$ has all its singular values greater than some $\gamma>2$ at every $x,y \in \mathbb{R}^d$--then their algorithm reaches a point $(x^\star, y^\star)$ where $\|
abla_x f(x^\star, y^\star)\| \leq \varepsilon$ and  $\|
abla_y f(x^\star, y^\star)\| \leq \varepsilon$ 
 in $O\left( rac{1}{\gamma^2} \log rac{M}{\varepsilon}ight)$ evaluations of a Hessian-vector product of $f$, where $M$ is the magnitude of  $
abla f$ at the point where their algorithm is initialized. ootnote{
Note that, since such algorithms' dynamics should ideally not be attracted to minima or maxima of $f$, additional assumptions on $f$ are typically needed even to show convergence to a first-order stationary point--that is, a point $(x^\star, y^\star)$ where $\|
abla_x f(x^\star, y^\star)\| \leq \varepsilon$ and  $\|
abla_y f(x^\star, y^\star)\| \leq \varepsilon$.}

assumptions: $f$ has $1$-Lipschitz gradient and satisfies a ``sufficient bilinearity'' condition
conclusions: their algorithm reaches a point $(x^\star, y^\star)$ where $\|\nabla_x f(x^\star, y^\star)\| \leq \varepsilon$ and  $\|\nabla_y f(x^\star, y^\star)\| \leq \varepsilon$
nodes.statement_short: Under sufficient bilinearity, a Hessian-vector method reaches a first-order stationary point in O(gamma^-2 log(M/eps)) evaluations.

nodes.name: Main result holds with greedy paths restricted to a ball
nodes.statement:
Theorem \ref{thm:GreedyMin-max} still holds if we restrict the greedy path to a ball whose radius is proportional to $\varepsilon$, $L_1$ and the distance $\|x-x^\star \|$ between $x^\star$ and the minimizing player's update $x$. 

This is because, roughly speaking, any greedy path that leaves this ball would reach a point $y$ for which the value of $f$ at $(x,y)$ is greater than the value of $f$ at $(x^\star, y^\star)$. 

This implies that the truncated greedy max function $\min(g_\varepsilon(x,y), g_\varepsilon(x^\star,y^\star))$ would have the exact same value regardless of whether we restrict the max-player to such a ball, and the point $(x^\star, y^\star)$ guaranteed by Theorem \ref{thm:GreedyMin-max} would therefore still satisfy Definition \ref{def:local_min-max_formal}.

nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.1 still holds when greedy paths are restricted to a ball of radius proportional to epsilon, L1 and ||x - x*||.

nodes.name: Nonexistence of solutions for the model of Jin et al.
nodes.statement:
The authors of \cite{minmax_Jordan} note that their model does not have any solution point on the function $f(x,y) = y^2 - 2xy$ on $[-1,1] \times [-1,1]$. 
 
  We can extend this function to a continuous function on all of $\mathbb{R}^2$ as follows. 
  
  Defining $\tilde{z} := | ((z+3) \mod 4) -2|-1$ for $z \in \mathbb{R}^2$, we have $f(x,y) = \tilde{y}^2 -2\tilde{x}\tilde{y}$  (in other words, we imagine that we put mirrors at each of the edges of the square $[-1,1] \times [-1,1]$, which reflect the value of the function across all of $\mathbb{R}^2$). 
  
    This function is uniformly bounded on all of $\mathbb{R}^2$ but does not have any point which is a solution point for the model in \cite{minmax_Jordan}.  
  
  We also note that one can smooth this function by convolution with a small-radius bump function of radius $r<\frac{1}{100}$, and these properties still hold for the smoothed function $\tilde{f}$.
  
  We can extend this example to many dimensions, for example by considering the objective function $\hat{f}(x,y) = \sum_{i=1}^d \tilde{f}(x_i,y_i)$.
nodes.section: 5.1 How does our greedy adversarial equilibrium compare to previous models?
nodes.statement_short: A mirrored extension of y^2 - 2xy is a bounded function with no solution point for the model of minmax_Jordan.
nodes.label: example_nonexistance

nodes.name: Equilibria persist under expanded max-player algorithm classes
nodes.statement: For this class of algorithms, any point $(x^\star, y^\star)$ which satisfies our original Definition \ref{def:local_min-max_formal}  also is a greedy adversarial equilibrium under this expanded definition.
nodes.section: 5.2 Applicability and limitations of our definition

nodes.name: Justification that equilibria persist under expanded algorithm classes
nodes.statement:
Roughly speaking, this is because as long as the max-player is at a local maximum for the function $f(x^\star,\cdot)$, expanding the choice of algorithms available to the max-player may increase the value of the greedy max function at points other than $x^\star$ but will not increase the value of the greedy max function at the current point $x^\star$. 

In other words, the minimizing player will not have an incentive to deviate from $x^\star$ if more algorithms are made available to the max-player.
nodes.section: 5.2 Applicability and limitations of our definition
nodes.statement_short: Extra algorithms that stop at local maxima cannot raise the greedy max at x*, so the min-player has no incentive to deviate.

nodes.name: Equilibria may fail for max-players using non-stopping algorithms
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if we allow the max-player to use algorithms which do not stop at local maxima, for instance algorithms such as simulated annealing, a solution  $(x^\star, y^\star)$ which satisfies our current definition may no longer be a solution in this expanded sense.
nodes.section: 5.2 Applicability and limitations of our definition

nodes.name: Justification for non-stopping algorithms
nodes.statement: This is because, giving the max-player the option to use algorithms which do not stop once a local maximum is reached may cause the greedy max function to increase at $x^\star$ more than at neighboring points, incentivizing the minimizing player to deviate from $x^\star$.
nodes.section: 5.2 Applicability and limitations of our definition
nodes.statement_short: Non-stopping algorithms can raise the greedy max at x* more than nearby, incentivizing deviation.

nodes.name: Justification of smoothness of Gaussian convolutions
nodes.statement: This is because a Gaussian density is $C^2$-smooth, and any function convolved with a $C^2$-smooth function is also $C^2$-smooth.

nodes.name: Derivative bounds for Gaussian smoothing
nodes.statement:
Moreover, if $\psi$ is $b$-bounded, then convolving $\psi$ with a Gaussian  gives a $b$-bounded function with the magnitude of its $k$'th-derivatives bounded by $2b$ times an upper bound on the $k$'th derivative of the standard Gaussian density, that is, $2b \times \frac{1}{\sigma^{2k+1} \sqrt{2 \pi}}$ for every $k>0$. 
    
     In particular, this means our smoothed function $\psi_\sigma(x)$ is also $b$-bounded, with $b \times \frac{1}{\sigma^{7} \sqrt{2 \pi}}$-Lipschitz Hessian (see Remark \ref{Rem_Lipschitz_convolution}).

conclusions: our smoothed function $\psi_\sigma(x)$ is also $b$-bounded, with $b \times \frac{1}{\sigma^{7} \sqrt{2 \pi}}$-Lipschitz Hessian

nodes.name: Gaussian smoothings are efficiently computable
nodes.statement: The family of functions $\mathcal{F}$ also has the advantage that, if $\psi$ is $b$-bounded, it can be computed within error $\varepsilon$ in $\mathrm{poly}(d,\nicefrac{1}{\varepsilon}, b)$ evaluations of $\psi$ with high probability if one uses a Monte-Carlo computation of the expectation $\mathbb{E}_{\zeta \sim N(0,I_d)}\left [\psi(x  + \sigma \zeta)\right]$, which satisfies our third property (3).

nodes.name: Convolution can shift local minima
nodes.statement:
Consider the function $\psi: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, where


 $   \psi(x)    = x - 3x \mathbbm{1}(x\leq 0) + \mathbbm{1}(x \leq 0).$
  
  
   This function is discontinuous at $x=0$, and has an exact local minimum at the point $x=0$ (which also happens to be its global minimum point). 
   
    If we smooth $\psi$ by convolving it with a Gaussian distribution $N(0,\sigma^2)$ for any $\sigma>0$,  we get the smooth function 
    
    \begin{equation*}
        \psi_\sigma(x) = 3 \sigma \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2 \sigma^2}} - x + x \Phi\left(\frac{1}{\sigma} x\right) + \Phi\left(-\frac{1}{\sigma} x\right),
         \end{equation*}
         
        where $\Phi(\cdot)$ is the standard Gaussian cumulative distribution function. 
   
    This function is $C^{2}$-smooth since $\Phi(\cdot)$ is $C^{2}$-smooth. 
    
    However, for any $\sigma >0$, the gradient at $x=0$ of the smoothed function is $-1.5 - \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2 \pi}}$. 
    
     Thus, for any $\sigma>0$, $x=0$ is not an approximate local minimum of the smoothed function for any parameter $\varepsilon \leq 1.5$.
nodes.section: 5.4 Additional discussion of approximate local minimum for discontinuous functions
nodes.statement_short: psi(x) = x - 3x 1(x<=0) + 1(x<=0) has a local minimum at 0, but its Gaussian smoothing has gradient magnitude >= 1.5 there.
nodes.label: ex_shifted_min1

nodes.name: Stochastic gradient formula for Gaussian smoothing
nodes.statement: \nabla \psi_\sigma(x) =   \frac{1}{\sigma} \mathbb{E}_{\zeta \sim N(0,I_d)}[(\psi(x + \sigma \zeta) - \psi(x)) \zeta].

nodes.name: Lipschitz and smoothness properties of convolution
nodes.statement:
If $\psi$ is a function and $\rho$ a probability distribution, then the convolution $\psi \ast \rho (x)$ of $\psi$ with $\rho$ is  defined as $\psi \ast \rho (x) := \mathbb{E}_{\zeta \sim \rho}\left [\psi(x  + \zeta)\right]$.  In one dimension, we can write this as the integral $\psi \ast \rho (x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \psi(x-t) \rho(t) \mathrm{d}t =  \int_{-\infty}^\infty \psi(t) \rho(x-t) \mathrm{d}t$. 

 Hence, if $\psi$ and $\rho$ are uniformly bounded then $\frac{\mathrm{d}^k}{\mathrm{d} x^k} \psi \ast \rho (x) =  \int_{-\infty}^\infty \psi(t) \frac{\mathrm{d}^k}{\mathrm{d} x^k} \rho(x-t) \mathrm{d}t$.
 
  Thus, if the distribution $\rho$ is $C^k$-smooth, then the convolution $\psi \ast \rho$ is also $C^k$-smooth. 
  
   Moreover, if $|\psi(x)| \leq b$  for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, and for any $k>0$ there is a number $c_k$ such that $\frac{\mathrm{d}^k}{\mathrm{d} x^k} \rho(x)| \leq c_k$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, then we must have that $|\frac{\mathrm{d}^k}{\mathrm{d} x^k} \psi \ast \rho (x)| \leq b \times c_k$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. 
   
    And, since $\psi$ is a probability distribution, we also have that $|\psi \ast \rho (x)| \leq b$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ whenever $|\psi(x)| \leq b$  for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. 
    
     In particular, if $\rho$ is the Gaussian distribution with variance $\sigma^2$, then its $k$'th derivative is bounded by $\frac{1}{\sigma^{2k+1} \sqrt{2 \pi}}$ for every $k$. 
    
     This implies that $\psi \ast \rho$ is $b$-bounded,  $2b \times \frac{1}{\sigma^{3} \sqrt{2 \pi}}$-Lipschitz, with $2b \times \frac{1}{\sigma^{5} \sqrt{2 \pi}}$-Lipschitz gradient and $2b \times \frac{1}{\sigma^{7} \sqrt{2 \pi}}$-Lipschitz Hessian. 
     
      The same argument can be extended to functions $\psi: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ of dimensions $d>1$.

nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we may assume that $b \geq 1$ (since our goal is to prove that the number of gradient evaluations is polynomial in $\frac{1}{\varepsilon}, d, b, L_{}, \frac{1}{\sigma}$).

nodes.name: Hyperparameters and constants
nodes.statement:
In our proof, we set the following hyperparameters and constants.


\begin{enumerate}

    \item $\omega := 10^{-3}$, 

\item $\gamma_1 := \frac{\varepsilon^{2.1} \sigma^{16.6}}{10^4 (1+b^{3.1}) d^{0.6} \log(b d \sigma \varepsilon)}$, 

\item $\delta := \frac{\gamma_1^2}{8 b^2}$, 

\item  $\mu_1 := \delta \frac{1}{L_2(L_1+1)}$,

\item $\mu_3 := \frac{1}{7}  \min\left( \frac{\delta \sqrt{\varepsilon}}{\sqrt{L_{}}}, \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{L_{}}} \right)$, 

 \item $\mu_4 := \frac{1}{7} \sqrt{\delta L_{} \varepsilon}$, 


\item $\eta := \frac{\sigma^9 }{  b^6 d^2 \left(1+ 10\frac{b d}{\sigma^{12}\varepsilon^2}\right) \mathsf{c} \log^9( bd\sqrt{\sigma \varepsilon})}$,  

\item $\mathcal{I}_2 := \frac{\mathsf{c} \log(bd\sqrt{\sigma \varepsilon})}{\eta \sqrt{\varepsilon}}$, 

\item $\mathcal{I}_3 := \frac{30 b}{\gamma_1}$,  

\item $\mathcal{I}_4 := 6\log\left(\frac{2 b}{\gamma_1 \omega}\right),$ 

 \item$\alpha := \eta \mathsf{c}\log( bd\sqrt{\sigma \varepsilon}) \sqrt{1+ b^2 d^2 \sigma^{-2}},$
 
 \end{enumerate}

 where $\mathsf{c}$ is a large enough universal constant.

nodes.name: Proof outline of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement:
The proof of Theorem \ref{thm:GreedyMin-max} has three main components:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item We start by showing that Algorithm \ref{alg:LocalMin-max} halts after $i^\star = O\left(\frac{b}{\gamma_1}\right)$ iterations, which allows us to bound the number of oracle calls until Algorithm \ref{alg:LocalMin-max} halts (Lemma \ref{lemma:RunningTime}).

\item We then show that the point $(x^\star, y^\star)$ returned by Algorithm \ref{alg:LocalMin-max} is an $(\varepsilon^\star, \sigma)$-greedy adversarial equilibrium for $f$, for some 

\begin{equation*}
\varepsilon^\star = \varepsilon_{i^\star} = \varepsilon_0 \leq  (1+\delta)^{O(i^\star)} \leq \varepsilon.
\end{equation*}

Towards this end we first show that $y^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon^\star, \sqrt{L \varepsilon^\star})$-approximate local maximum of $f(x^\star, \cdot)$ (in the sense of the definition in \eqref{eq:ApproximateLocalMin_formal}) and therefore satisfies Inequalities \eqref{eq:first_order_y} of Definition \ref{def:local_min-max_formal}.

\item Next, we show that $x^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon^\star, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum of  $g_\varepsilon(\cdot, y^\star))$ (in the sense of Definition \ref{def_discontinuos_local_min}), and therefore satisfies Inequalities \eqref{eq:first_order_x} of Definition \ref{def:local_min-max_formal} (see the proof in Section \ref{concluding_the_proof}).

Towards this end, we prove (in Lemma \ref{Lemma_SharedLM}) that to guarantee  $x^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon^\star, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum of  $g_\varepsilon(\cdot, y^\star)$, it is sufficient to show that $x^\star$ is an $(\varepsilon^\star, \sigma)$-approximate local minimum of  $h_\varepsilon(\cdot, y^\star)$ (Propositions \ref{Prop_first_order_x} and \ref{Prop_NoisySGD}), provided that we can also show that $h_\varepsilon$ and $g_\varepsilon$ satisfy a number of conditions.

Namely, these conditions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $h_\varepsilon(x,y) \leq g_\varepsilon(x,y)$ for all $(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d$ (Proposition \ref{Prop_lower_bound}).
    
    \item $h_\varepsilon(x^\star,y^\star) = g_\varepsilon(x^\star,y^\star)$ (Proposition \ref{Prop_fixed_point}).
    
    \item A stochastic gradient for a smoothed version of $h_\varepsilon$  (defined in Equation \eqref{eq_SG_H}) has a very small expected magnitude (Proposition \ref{prop_SGVariance}).
nodes.statement_short: Outline: bound the running time, show y* is an approximate local max, and reduce minimality of x* for g_eps to that for h_eps via Lemma 7.3.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7.1
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Bounding the iterations of Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop}}:
First, we bound the number of iterations of the  ``While" loop in Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop}. 

We begin by showing that $\| \nabla_y f(\mathsf{x}, \mathsf{y}^{\ell})\| > \varepsilon'$ occurs at least once every $\frac{4 \varepsilon'}{\mu_3^2 L_{}}$ iterations.

Consider any iteration $\ell$ where $\| \nabla_y f(\mathsf{x}, \mathsf{y}^{\ell})\| \leq \varepsilon'$.  Then (unless Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop} terminates at step $\ell$ of the While loop) Line \ref{GreedyEnpoint_Start} of Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop} implies that we have both
\begin{equation*}
v^\top \nabla^2_{{y}}f(\mathsf{x}, \mathsf{y}^{\ell}) v \geq \sqrt{L_{} \varepsilon'},

\quad \textrm{ and } \quad
 
 \mathsf{y}^{\ell+1} = \mathsf{y}^\ell + \mu_3 \mathsf{a} v,
\end{equation*}
 
 where $\mathsf{a} = \mathrm{sign}(\nabla_yf(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}^{\ell})^\top v)$.
\noindent 
  Hence, since $\mu_3 \leq \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon'}}{2\sqrt{L_{}}}$, we have that
  
\begin{align*}
\nabla_y f(\mathsf{x}, \mathsf{y}^{\ell+1}) - \nabla_y f(\mathsf{x}, \mathsf{y}^{\ell}) &\geq  [\nabla_y^2 f(\mathsf{x}, \mathsf{y}^{\ell}) -L_{} \mu_3 I_d] \mu_3 \mathsf{a} v\\

&= (\sqrt{L_{} \varepsilon'} - L_{} \mu_3) \mu_3 \mathsf{a} v\\

&\geq  \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{L_{} \varepsilon'} \mu_3 \mathsf{a} v.
\end{align*}


\noindent
Therefore, since $\mathsf{a} = \mathrm{sign}(\nabla_yf(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y}^{\ell})^\top v)$, we have that,
\begin{equs} \|\nabla_y f(\mathsf{x}, \mathsf{y}^{\ell+1})\|^2 - \|\nabla_y f(\mathsf{x}, \mathsf{y}^{\ell})\|^2 \geq  \left(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{L_{} \varepsilon'} \mu_3 \right)^2.
\end{equs}
Therefore, we have that the magnitude of the gradient becomes $\geq \varepsilon'$ at least once every $\mathfrak{c} := \frac{4 \varepsilon'}{\mu_3^2 L_{}}$ iterations of the While loop of Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop}. 

Since $\mu_3 \leq \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}{4\sqrt{L_{}}} \leq \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon'}}{2\sqrt{L_{}}}$, for some unit vector $w$ we have that
\begin{equs} f(\mathsf{x}, \mathsf{y}^{\ell+1}) -  f(\mathsf{x}, \mathsf{y}^{\ell})
 
 &\geq \mu_3 \mathsf{a} \nabla_y f(\mathsf{x}, \mathsf{y}^{\ell}) ^\top v  + \frac{1}{2} \mu_3^2 v^\top (\nabla_y ^2 f(\mathsf{x}, \mathsf{y}^{\ell}) - \mu_3 L_{} I_d) v\\
 
  &\geq 0  + \frac{1}{2} \mu_3^2 \sqrt{L_{} \varepsilon'}  - \frac{1}{2} \mu_3^3 L_{} 

  \geq \frac{1}{4} \mu_3^2 \sqrt{L_{} \varepsilon'} \geq 0.
 \end{equs}
 
Recall that we have also shown (Inequality \eqref{eq:a1}) that the gradient becomes $\geq \varepsilon'$ at least once every $\mathfrak{c} := \frac{4 \varepsilon'}{\mu_3^2 L_{}}$ iterations of the While loop of Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop}.  Therefore, since $\mu_1 \leq \frac{1}{2 L_2}$ and $f$ is uniformly bounded by $b$, we must have that the While loop in Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop} terminates after $O\left(\frac{b \mathfrak{c} }{\mu_1 \varepsilon}\right)$ iterations, and hence that  Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop} terminates after $O\left(\frac{b}{ \mu_1 \mu_3^2 L_{}}\right)$ oracle evaluations.

\bigskip


\noindent
\textbf{Bounding the iterations of Algorithm \ref{alg:LocalMin-max}}:

At each iteration $i$ of the While loop in Algorithm \ref{alg:LocalMin-max} except for the last iteration $i^\star$, Lines \ref{HillClimbing} and \ref{SuccessStart} of Algorithm \ref{alg:LocalMin-max} imply that
\begin{equs} f(x_{i+1}, y_{i+1}) \leq f(x_{i}, y_{i}) - \gamma_1.
\end{equs}

\noindent
Therefore, since $f$ is uniformly bounded  by $b$, Inequality \eqref{eq:a5} implies that the While loop of Algorithm \ref{alg:LocalMin-max} terminates after at most $i_{\max}$ iterations for some number $i_{\max} = O\left(\frac{b}{\gamma_1}\right)$. 

 Therefore since we have already shown that Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop} terminates in at most $O\left(\frac{b}{ \mu_1 \mu_3^2 L_{}}\right)$ oracle calls each time it is called, and Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop} is called $\mathcal{I}_3 + \mathcal{I}_2 \mathcal{I}_4$ times at each iteration of the While loop, running Algorithm \ref{alg:InnerMaxLoop} contributes at most $O\left(\frac{b}{\gamma_1} \times (\mathcal{I}_3 + \mathcal{I}_2 \mathcal{I}_4)  \times \frac{b}{ \mu_1 \mu_3^2 L_{}} \right)$ oracle calls to the cost of Algorithm \ref{alg:LocalMin-max}. 
 
  Since the other parts of the While loop make at most $O(\mathcal{I}_3 + \mathcal{I}_2 \mathcal{I}_4)$ function evaluations, they contribute no more that $O\left(\frac{b}{\gamma_1} \times (\mathcal{I}_3 + \mathcal{I}_2 \mathcal{I}_4)\right)$ function evaluations to the cost of Algorithm \ref{alg:LocalMin-max}. 
  
  Therefore, Algorithm \ref{alg:LocalMin-max} terminates after at most $O\left(\frac{b}{\gamma_1} \times (\mathcal{I}_3 + \mathcal{I}_2 \mathcal{I}_4) \times \frac{b}{ \mu_1 \mu_3^2 L_{}}\right)$ oracle calls.
nodes.statement_short: Each inner step raises f or the gradient norm by a fixed amount and f is bounded; each outer iteration lowers f by gamma1. The key step is that the gradient exceeds eps' at least once every 4eps'/(mu3^2 L) inner iterations.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7.3
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Showing first-order condition holds:}

First, note that
\begin{equs}
&\mathbbm{h}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x,y^\star) = \left [\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\right]\\
&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c11}}{\leq} \min(g_{\varepsilon}(x, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c7}}{=} \min(g_{\varepsilon}(x, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\\
&= \mathbbm{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x,y^\star)  \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d.
\end{equs}


\noindent
Define the stochastic gradient $\mathcal{G}(x,y):= \frac{\zeta}{\sigma}(\mathbbm{g}_\varepsilon^{x^\star}(x  + \sigma \zeta,y) - \mathbbm{g}_\varepsilon^{x^\star}(x ,y))$ for all $x,y \in \mathbb{R}^d$, where $\zeta \sim N(0,I_d)$.

 Since $\mathbbm{h}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}$ and  $\mathbbm{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}$  are uniformly bounded, by Lemma 7 of \cite{zhang2017hitting}, we have that 
\begin{equation*}
\nabla_{{x}} \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) = \mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{H}_\varepsilon^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)\right],
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
 \qquad \nabla_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) := \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathcal{G}(x^\star, y^\star) \right].
\end{equation*}


\noindent
Inequality \eqref{eq:c8} implies that
\begin{equs} \frac{1}{8000}  \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2} &\geq \mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathcal{H}_\varepsilon^{x^\star}(x^\star,y^\star)\right\|\right]\\

&= \mathbb{E} [\| \zeta \sigma^{-1}  (\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) - \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\|]\\


&=\mathbb{E}[\|\zeta \sigma^{-1} (\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)\|]\\

&= \mathbb{E} [\|\zeta\| \sigma^{-1}\times  |\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) |]\\

&\geq\mathbb{E}[\|\zeta\| \sigma^{-1}] \times \mathbb{E}[  | \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)  |]\\

&= \sqrt{d}\sigma^{-1} \mathbb{E}[  | \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) |]\\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c7}}{=}  \sqrt{d}\sigma^{-1} \mathbb{E}[ \left | \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) \right |]\\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c11}}{\geq}\sqrt{d}\sigma^{-1} \mathbb{E}[ |\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) |],
\end{equs}

where the second inequality holds since $E[XY] \geq E[X] E[Y]$ for any nonnegative random variables $X, Y$. 

The last inequality holds since $\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) \leq 0$ and since Inequality \eqref{eq:c11} implies that $h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star) \leq g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star)$.

  Thus,
\begin{equs} 
\|&\nabla_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)\|\\

&=  \| \mathbb{E}_{\zeta\sim N(0,I_d)}[\zeta \sigma^{-1} (\mathbbm{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta,y^\star) - \mathbbm{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x^\star,y^\star))]  \|\\

&=  \| \mathbb{E}_{\zeta\sim N(0,I_d)}[\zeta \sigma^{-1} (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) - \min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))] \| \\

&=  \|\mathbb{E}_{\zeta\sim N(0,I_d)}[\zeta \sigma^{-1} (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))]\|\\
&\leq \mathbb{E}[ \|\zeta \sigma^{-1} (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\| ]\\

&= \mathbb{E}\left[ \|\zeta \sigma^{-1}\| \times  | (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))| \right]\\

&\leq \mathbb{E}\left[ \sqrt{d} \sigma^{-1}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \times | (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))| \right]\\

&\qquad \qquad \qquad +\mathbb{P}\left(\|\zeta\| \geq  \sqrt{d}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \right) \times \mathbb{E}\left[ \| \zeta \sigma^{-1} \| \times 2b  \, \, \,\, \,  \,   \bigg | \, \,  \,  \, \,  \,  \|\zeta\| \geq  \sqrt{d}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \right]\\

&\leq \mathbb{E}\left[ \sqrt{d} \sigma^{-1}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \times | (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))| \right]\\

&\qquad \qquad \qquad + 2 \left(\frac{\varepsilon \sigma}{10 b \sqrt{d}}\right)^2 \times \mathbb{E}\left[ \| \zeta \sigma^{-1} \| b  \, \, \, \, \, \, \bigg | \, \, \, \, \, \,  \|\zeta\| \geq  \sqrt{d}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \right]\\

&\leq \mathbb{E}\left[ \sqrt{d} \sigma^{-1} \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \times | (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))| \right]\\

&\qquad \qquad \qquad + 4 \left(\frac{\varepsilon \sigma}{10 b \sqrt{d}}\right)^2 \sigma^{-1}  b \sqrt{d} \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right)\\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c1}}{\leq}
\frac{1}{8000}  \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) + 4 \left(\frac{\varepsilon \sigma}{10 b \sqrt{d}}\right)^2 \sigma^{-1}  b \sqrt{d} \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right)\\

&\leq \varepsilon,
\end{equs}
\noindent

 where the third and fourth inequalities hold by a standard concentration bound for Gaussians \cite{hanson1971bound}, and the last inequality holds because $\sigma \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon d}}$, $b\geq 1$, and  $\sigma, \varepsilon \leq 1$.

This shows inequality \eqref{eq:c2}.\\

\noindent \textbf{Showing that second-order condition holds:}

First, we will show that, roughly speaking, $\mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) \approx \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)$.   Since $g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) = h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)$, we have, by Inequality \eqref{eq:c1} that

\begin{equs} 0 &\leq g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) - \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)\\

&=  \mathbb{E}[ g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) - \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))]  \\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c7}}{=}  \mathbb{E}[ g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) - \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))] \\

&= \mathbb{E}[|g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) - \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))|] \\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c1}}{\leq} \frac{1}{8000} \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{d}},
\end{equs}

and

\begin{equs} 0 &\geq \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) - g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)\\

&=  \mathbb{E}[\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)]  \\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c1}}{\geq} -\frac{1}{8000} \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{d}}.
\end{equs}
Thus, \eqref{eq:c5} and \eqref{eq:c21} together  with \eqref{eq:c11} and \eqref{eq:c7} imply that

\begin{equation} 0 \leq \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) -  \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) \leq \frac{1}{4000} \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{d}}

\leq \frac{1}{4000} \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}},
\end{equation}

where the last inequality holds since $\sigma \leq 1$.

\noindent \textbf{Contradiction argument:}
We will show \eqref{eq:c3} by contradiction.  Towards this end, suppose that the following statement were true
\begin{equs} \lambda_{\mathrm{min}}(\nabla^2_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)) < - \sqrt{\varepsilon}.
\end{equs}
Then there would exist a unit vector $v$ such that
\begin{equs} v^\top \nabla^2_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) v < - \sqrt{\varepsilon}.
\end{equs}
Let $\hat{\mathsf{a}} := \mathrm{sign}(\nabla_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)^\top v)$.  Then, since $\mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}$ has $\frac{2b}{\sigma^7}$-Lipschitz Hessian (see Remark \ref{Rem_Lipschitz_convolution}), for every $t \geq 0$ we have

\begin{equs} &\mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}} v, y^\star) - \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)\\

&\leq \frac{1}{2} t^2 v^\top \left(\nabla^2_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) + t \frac{2b}{\sigma^7} I_d\right) v

\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c20}}{\leq}  - \frac{1}{2}  t^2 \left(\sqrt{\varepsilon} - t \frac{2b}{\sigma^7}\right).
\end{equs}
\noindent
Consider the value $t=  \frac{\sigma^{7} \sqrt{\varepsilon}}{20 b}$.  Then Inequality \eqref{eq:c22} implies that
\begin{equs} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}}v, y^\star) - \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) &\leq -\frac{\nicefrac{9}{2}}{4000} \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2}.
\end{equs}

\noindent
But we also have from our assumption (Inequality \eqref{eq:c10}) that
\begin{equs} v^\top \nabla^2_{{x}} \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) v \geq - \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}{5}.
\end{equs}
 Then, since $\mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}$ has $\frac{2b}{\sigma^7}$-Lipschitz Hessian (see Remark \ref{Rem_Lipschitz_convolution}), for $t= \frac{\sigma^{7} \sqrt{\varepsilon}}{20 b}$ we have

\begin{equs} &\mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}} v, y^\star) - \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)\\

&\geq \frac{t^2}{2} v^\top \left(\nabla^2_{{x}} \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) - t\frac{2b}{\sigma^7} I_d\right) v -t \hat{\mathsf{a}} \nabla_{{x}} \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star )^\top v \\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c13}, \ref{eq:c23}}{\geq}  - \frac{t^2 }{2} \left(\frac{1}{5}\sqrt{\varepsilon} + t\frac{2b}{\sigma^7}\right) -  \frac{1}{8000}  \frac{\varepsilon^2 \sigma^7}{ b} t

\geq -  \frac{2 \sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{4000 \, b^2}.
\end{equs}

\noindent Combining Inequalities \eqref{eq:c6},  \eqref{eq:c12} and \eqref{eq:c14}, we get that

\begin{equs}
&\mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}}v, y^\star) - \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}}v, y^\star)\\ &\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c6},\ref{eq:c12},\ref{eq:c14}}{\leq}   \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)  - \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)  -\frac{5}{2}\times \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{4000 \, b^2}.\\
& \stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c6}}{\leq}  -\frac{3}{2}\times \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{4000 \, b^2},
\end{equs}
which implies that
\begin{equs} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}}v, y^\star) < \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}}v, y^\star).
\end{equs}


\noindent Now, we also have that 
\begin{equs} &\mathbbm{h}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x,y^\star) = \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\\
&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c11}}{\leq}  \min(g_{\varepsilon}(x, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))

\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c7}}{=}  \min(g_{\varepsilon}(x, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\\
&= \mathbbm{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x,y^\star)  \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d.
\end{equs}
and hence that
\begin{equs} &\mathfrak{h}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x,y^\star) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbbm{h}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x+\sigma \zeta ,y^\star) ]\\

&\leq  \mathbb{E}[\mathbbm{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x+\sigma \zeta ,y^\star) ]= \mathfrak{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x,y^\star)  \qquad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d.
\end{equs}

\noindent Since inequality \eqref{eq:c17} contradicts Inequality \eqref{eq:c15}, our Assumption (Inequality \eqref{eq:c4}) must be false.  Therefore we have
\begin{equs}
\lambda_{\mathrm{min}}(\nabla^2_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)) \geq - \sqrt{\varepsilon},
\end{equs}
which completes the proof of the second-order condition \eqref{eq:c3}.

\textbf{Showing first-order condition holds:}

First, note that
\begin{equs}
&\mathbbm{h}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x,y^\star) = \left [\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\right]\\
&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c11}}{\leq} \min(g_{\varepsilon}(x, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c7}}{=} \min(g_{\varepsilon}(x, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\\
&= \mathbbm{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x,y^\star)  \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d.
\end{equs}


\noindent
Define the stochastic gradient $\mathcal{G}(x,y):= \frac{\zeta}{\sigma}(\mathbbm{g}_\varepsilon^{x^\star}(x  + \sigma \zeta,y) - \mathbbm{g}_\varepsilon^{x^\star}(x ,y))$ for all $x,y \in \mathbb{R}^d$, where $\zeta \sim N(0,I_d)$.

 Since $\mathbbm{h}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}$ and  $\mathbbm{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}$  are uniformly bounded, by Lemma 7 of \cite{zhang2017hitting}, we have that 
\begin{equation*}

\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
 \qquad \nabla_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) := \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathcal{G}(x^\star, y^\star) \right].
\end{equation*}

Inequality \eqref{eq:c8} implies that

&= \mathbb{E} [\| \zeta \sigma^{-1}  (\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) - \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\|]\\


&=\mathbb{E}[\|\zeta \sigma^{-1} (\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)\|]\\

&= \mathbb{E} [\|\zeta\| \sigma^{-1}\times  |\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) |]\\

&\geq\mathbb{E}[\|\zeta\| \sigma^{-1}] \times \mathbb{E}[  | \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)  |]\\

&= \sqrt{d}\sigma^{-1} \mathbb{E}[  | \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) |]\\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c7}}{=}  \sqrt{d}\sigma^{-1} \mathbb{E}[ \left | \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) \right |]\\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c11}}{\geq}\sqrt{d}\sigma^{-1} \mathbb{E}[ |\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) |],
\end{equs}

where the second inequality holds since $E[XY] \geq E[X] E[Y]$ for any nonnegative random variables $X, Y$. 

The last inequality holds since $\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) \leq 0$ and since Inequality \eqref{eq:c11} implies that $h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star) \leq g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star)$.

  Thus,
\begin{equs} 
\|&\nabla_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)\|\\

&=  \| \mathbb{E}_{\zeta\sim N(0,I_d)}[\zeta \sigma^{-1} (\mathbbm{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta,y^\star) - \mathbbm{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x^\star,y^\star))]  \|\\

&=  \| \mathbb{E}_{\zeta\sim N(0,I_d)}[\zeta \sigma^{-1} (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) - \min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))] \| \\

&=  \|\mathbb{E}_{\zeta\sim N(0,I_d)}[\zeta \sigma^{-1} (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))]\|\\
&\leq \mathbb{E}[ \|\zeta \sigma^{-1} (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\| ]\\

&= \mathbb{E}\left[ \|\zeta \sigma^{-1}\| \times  | (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))| \right]\\

&\leq \mathbb{E}\left[ \sqrt{d} \sigma^{-1}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \times | (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))| \right]\\

&\qquad \qquad \qquad +\mathbb{P}\left(\|\zeta\| \geq  \sqrt{d}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \right) \times \mathbb{E}\left[ \| \zeta \sigma^{-1} \| \times 2b  \, \, \,\, \,  \,   \bigg | \, \,  \,  \, \,  \,  \|\zeta\| \geq  \sqrt{d}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \right]\\

&\leq \mathbb{E}\left[ \sqrt{d} \sigma^{-1}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \times | (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))| \right]\\

&\qquad \qquad \qquad + 2 \left(\frac{\varepsilon \sigma}{10 b \sqrt{d}}\right)^2 \times \mathbb{E}\left[ \| \zeta \sigma^{-1} \| b  \, \, \, \, \, \, \bigg | \, \, \, \, \, \,  \|\zeta\| \geq  \sqrt{d}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \right]\\

&\leq \mathbb{E}\left[ \sqrt{d} \sigma^{-1} \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \times | (\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))| \right]\\

&\qquad \qquad \qquad + 4 \left(\frac{\varepsilon \sigma}{10 b \sqrt{d}}\right)^2 \sigma^{-1}  b \sqrt{d} \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right)\\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c1}}{\leq}
\frac{1}{8000}  \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) + 4 \left(\frac{\varepsilon \sigma}{10 b \sqrt{d}}\right)^2 \sigma^{-1}  b \sqrt{d} \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right)\\

&\leq \varepsilon,
\end{equs}
\noindent

 where the third and fourth inequalities hold by a standard concentration bound for Gaussians \cite{hanson1971bound}, and the last inequality holds because $\sigma \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon d}}$, $b\geq 1$, and  $\sigma, \varepsilon \leq 1$.

This shows inequality \eqref{eq:c2}.

&= \mathbb{E} [\| \zeta \sigma^{-1}  (\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) - \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\|]\\


&=\mathbb{E}[\|\zeta \sigma^{-1} (\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)\|]\\

&= \mathbb{E} [\|\zeta\| \sigma^{-1}\times  |\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) |]\\

&\geq\mathbb{E}[\|\zeta\| \sigma^{-1}] \times \mathbb{E}[  | \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)  |]\\

&= \sqrt{d}\sigma^{-1} \mathbb{E}[  | \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) |]\\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c7}}{=}  \sqrt{d}\sigma^{-1} \mathbb{E}[ \left | \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) \right |]\\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c11}}{\geq}\sqrt{d}\sigma^{-1} \mathbb{E}[ |\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) |],
\end{equs}

where the second inequality holds since $E[XY] \geq E[X] E[Y]$ for any nonnegative random variables $X, Y$. 

The last inequality holds since $\min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) \leq 0$ and since Inequality \eqref{eq:c11} implies that $h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star) \leq g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star)$.

&\qquad \qquad \qquad +\mathbb{P}\left(\|\zeta\| \geq  \sqrt{d}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \right) \times \mathbb{E}\left[ \| \zeta \sigma^{-1} \| \times 2b  \, \, \,\, \,  \,   \bigg | \, \,  \,  \, \,  \,  \|\zeta\| \geq  \sqrt{d}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \right]\\

&\qquad \qquad \qquad + 2 \left(\frac{\varepsilon \sigma}{10 b \sqrt{d}}\right)^2 \times \mathbb{E}\left[ \| \zeta \sigma^{-1} \| b  \, \, \, \, \, \, \bigg | \, \, \, \, \, \,  \|\zeta\| \geq  \sqrt{d}  \log\left(\left(\frac{10 b \sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon \sigma}\right)^2\right) \right]\\

&\leq \varepsilon,
\end{equs}

 where the third and fourth inequalities hold by a standard concentration bound for Gaussians \cite{hanson1971bound}, and the last inequality holds because $\sigma \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon d}}$, $b\geq 1$, and  $\sigma, \varepsilon \leq 1$.

\textbf{Showing that second-order condition holds:}

First, we will show that, roughly speaking, $\mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) \approx \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)$.   Since $g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) = h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)$, we have, by Inequality \eqref{eq:c1} that

\begin{equs} 0 &\leq g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) - \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)\\

&=  \mathbb{E}[ g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) - \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))]  \\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c7}}{=}  \mathbb{E}[ g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) - \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))] \\

&= \mathbb{E}[|g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star) - \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))|] \\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c1}}{\leq} \frac{1}{8000} \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{d}},
\end{equs}

and

\begin{equs} 0 &\geq \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) - g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)\\

&=  \mathbb{E}[\min(g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star+ \sigma \zeta, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)) -  g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star)]  \\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c1}}{\geq} -\frac{1}{8000} \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{d}}.
\end{equs}
Thus, \eqref{eq:c5} and \eqref{eq:c21} together  with \eqref{eq:c11} and \eqref{eq:c7} imply that

\begin{equation} 0 \leq \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) -  \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) \leq \frac{1}{4000} \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{d}}

\leq \frac{1}{4000} \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}},
\end{equation}

where the last inequality holds since $\sigma \leq 1$.

nodes.name: Contradiction argument
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Contradiction argument:}
We will show \eqref{eq:c3} by contradiction.  Towards this end, suppose that the following statement were true
\begin{equs} \lambda_{\mathrm{min}}(\nabla^2_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)) < - \sqrt{\varepsilon}.
\end{equs}
Then there would exist a unit vector $v$ such that
\begin{equs} v^\top \nabla^2_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) v < - \sqrt{\varepsilon}.
\end{equs}
Let $\hat{\mathsf{a}} := \mathrm{sign}(\nabla_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)^\top v)$.  Then, since $\mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}$ has $\frac{2b}{\sigma^7}$-Lipschitz Hessian (see Remark \ref{Rem_Lipschitz_convolution}), for every $t \geq 0$ we have

\begin{equs} &\mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}} v, y^\star) - \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)\\

&\leq \frac{1}{2} t^2 v^\top \left(\nabla^2_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) + t \frac{2b}{\sigma^7} I_d\right) v

\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c20}}{\leq}  - \frac{1}{2}  t^2 \left(\sqrt{\varepsilon} - t \frac{2b}{\sigma^7}\right).
\end{equs}
\noindent
Consider the value $t=  \frac{\sigma^{7} \sqrt{\varepsilon}}{20 b}$.  Then Inequality \eqref{eq:c22} implies that
\begin{equs} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}}v, y^\star) - \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) &\leq -\frac{\nicefrac{9}{2}}{4000} \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{b^2}.
\end{equs}

\noindent
But we also have from our assumption (Inequality \eqref{eq:c10}) that
\begin{equs} v^\top \nabla^2_{{x}} \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) v \geq - \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}{5}.
\end{equs}
 Then, since $\mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}$ has $\frac{2b}{\sigma^7}$-Lipschitz Hessian (see Remark \ref{Rem_Lipschitz_convolution}), for $t= \frac{\sigma^{7} \sqrt{\varepsilon}}{20 b}$ we have

\begin{equs} &\mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}} v, y^\star) - \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)\\

&\geq \frac{t^2}{2} v^\top \left(\nabla^2_{{x}} \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star) - t\frac{2b}{\sigma^7} I_d\right) v -t \hat{\mathsf{a}} \nabla_{{x}} \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star )^\top v \\

&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c13}, \ref{eq:c23}}{\geq}  - \frac{t^2 }{2} \left(\frac{1}{5}\sqrt{\varepsilon} + t\frac{2b}{\sigma^7}\right) -  \frac{1}{8000}  \frac{\varepsilon^2 \sigma^7}{ b} t

\geq -  \frac{2 \sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{4000 \, b^2}.
\end{equs}

\noindent Combining Inequalities \eqref{eq:c6},  \eqref{eq:c12} and \eqref{eq:c14}, we get that

\begin{equs}
&\mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}}v, y^\star) - \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}}v, y^\star)\\ &\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c6},\ref{eq:c12},\ref{eq:c14}}{\leq}   \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)  - \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)  -\frac{5}{2}\times \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{4000 \, b^2}.\\
& \stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c6}}{\leq}  -\frac{3}{2}\times \frac{\sigma^{14} \varepsilon^{1.5}}{4000 \, b^2},
\end{equs}
which implies that
\begin{equs} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}}v, y^\star) < \mathfrak{h}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star - t \hat{\mathsf{a}}v, y^\star).
\end{equs}


\noindent Now, we also have that 
\begin{equs} &\mathbbm{h}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x,y^\star) = \min(h_{\varepsilon}(x, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\\
&\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c11}}{\leq}  \min(g_{\varepsilon}(x, y^\star), h_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))

\stackrel{\textrm{Eq.} \ref{eq:c7}}{=}  \min(g_{\varepsilon}(x, y^\star), g_{\varepsilon}(x^\star, y^\star))\\
&= \mathbbm{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x,y^\star)  \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d.
\end{equs}
and hence that
\begin{equs} &\mathfrak{h}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x,y^\star) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbbm{h}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x+\sigma \zeta ,y^\star) ]\\

&\leq  \mathbb{E}[\mathbbm{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x+\sigma \zeta ,y^\star) ]= \mathfrak{g}^{x^\star}_{\varepsilon}(x,y^\star)  \qquad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d.
\end{equs}

\noindent Since inequality \eqref{eq:c17} contradicts Inequality \eqref{eq:c15}, our Assumption (Inequality \eqref{eq:c4}) must be false.  Therefore we have
\begin{equs}
\lambda_{\mathrm{min}}(\nabla^2_{{x}} \mathfrak{g}_{\varepsilon, \sigma}^{x^\star}(x^\star, y^\star)) \geq - \sqrt{\varepsilon},
\end{equs}
which completes the proof of the second-order condition \eqref{eq:c3}.
nodes.statement_short: Second-order condition by contradiction.

\end{equs}
for some unit vectors $u, w$, since $\mu_1 \leq (1-  rac{1}{1+\delta})  rac{1}{2 L_2}$.
nodes.statement_short: On gradient steps the directional derivative exceeds eps'/(1+delta).

nodes.name: Curvature steps
nodes.statement_short: On curvature steps the second derivative exceeds sqrt(L eps'/(1+delta)).
